comparison: Perfect agreement on inducible knockout experiments (C106-C117). Both recognize this as a critical control demonstrating developmental programming. Reviewers view this as a major strength showing that adult phenotypes require embryonic SPAG7 loss, while OpenEval emphasizes the complete absence of metabolic phenotypes in iSPAG7 KO animals.

Both address the developmental programming hypothesis linking IUGR to adult obesity (C15, C178-C181). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN, noting the hypothesis is plausible but speculative with lacking direct mechanistic evidence. Peer reviewers SUPPORT this interpretation as reasonable, accepting the 'thrifty phenotype' connection without challenging the mechanistic gaps.

Strong agreement on the connection between fetal development and adult metabolic state (C190-C195). Both recognize this as a central finding. OpenEval views it as an accurate summary of well-documented phenotypes, while peer reviewers emphasize the fundamental role of in-utero development in setting future metabolic state.

Both support the overarching conclusion about SPAG7's role in placental development and metabolism (C16, C187-C189). OpenEval emphasizes the first in vivo functional characterization claim, while peer reviewers unanimously view this as filling a knowledge gap with implications beyond metabolism including embryonic and placental development.

Both strongly support the novelty and significance of SPAG7 functional characterization (C196-C197). OpenEval confirms the 'first in vivo' claim appears accurate, while peer reviewers unanimously agree the work fills a knowledge gap and is important in terms of significance.

Both support the obesity phenotype and biphasic growth pattern (C3, C41-C44, C46). OpenEval emphasizes the robust statistical evidence and longitudinal documentation, while peer reviewers consistently acknowledge the progression from low birth weight to adult obesity without questioning the growth curve data.

Both support the metabolic dysfunction findings (C4, C67-C70). OpenEval highlights the convergence of GTT/ITT data with appropriate statistics, while peer reviewers consistently acknowledge impaired glucose tolerance and insulin sensitivity as major metabolic abnormalities accompanying the phenotype.

Both support the finding that obesity occurs without hyperphagia (C5, C71-C72). OpenEval emphasizes BioDaq food intake monitoring data, while peer reviewers consistently note that increased adiposity was not due to increased food intake, distinguishing this from other obesity models.

Strong agreement on reduced energy expenditure as the primary driver (C6, C73-C76, C85). OpenEval emphasizes CLAMS data and consistency across conditions, while peer reviewers view decreased energy expenditure at both room temperature and thermoneutrality as central to the phenotype.

Both support the thermoneutrality experiments ruling out thermogenesis (C77-C81). OpenEval views this as effectively ruling out thermogenesis as a major contributor, while peer reviewers accept these experiments as part of comprehensive metabolic characterization supporting the energy expenditure mechanism.

Both support the high-fat diet experiments (C82-C84). OpenEval emphasizes the consistency of weight gain percentage (15-17%) across conditions as strongly supporting reduced locomotor activity, while peer reviewers accept these data as additional support for the energy expenditure mechanism.

Both support the exercise capacity deficits (C7, C86-C87). OpenEval emphasizes treadmill endurance and VO2 max data as part of converging evidence for mitochondrial dysfunction, while peer reviewers acknowledge compromised exercise endurance and muscle functionality without specific concerns about the data.

Both support the muscle dysfunction findings (C8, C88-C90). OpenEval highlights in vivo force generation and histology data, while peer reviewers accept muscle functionality deficits stemming from mitochondrial deterioration and correlating with decreased locomotor activity and muscle atrophy.

Strong agreement on mitochondrial dysfunction (C9, C93-C94, C97, C105). OpenEval emphasizes the convergence of multiple assays and RNAseq data with GO enrichment analysis, while peer reviewers consistently acknowledge mitochondrial activity deterioration and view transcriptomic analysis as a strength.

Both support muscle characterization findings (C91-C92). OpenEval includes these as part of comprehensive muscle analysis with histology and SDH staining, while peer reviewers accept these findings without specific comment as supporting data for muscle dysfunction.

Both support the transcriptomic analysis (C95-C96). OpenEval emphasizes RNAseq data (n=7, 2,291 downregulated genes) providing mechanistic insight, while peer reviewers view the transcriptomic analysis of skeletal muscle as imparting substantial value and a study strength.

Both support the Hsd17b10 findings (C98-C104). OpenEval finds the connection intriguing given its role in mitochondrial tRNA maturation though notes causal relationship requires further investigation, while peer reviewers accept these findings as part of transcriptomic analysis supporting mitochondrial dysfunction.

Both support the Hsd17b10 background information (C99-C103). OpenEval views these as accurately cited facts helping interpret RNAseq findings with noteworthy parallels to HSD10 disease, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the transcriptomic analysis without specific discussion.

Both support the birth phenotype findings (C2, C118-C120). OpenEval emphasizes systematic genotyping and statistical analysis, while peer reviewers consistently acknowledge diminished birth size, decreased organ sizes, and lower birth weight without concerns about these data.

Both support the IUGR phenotype (C10, C126-C128). OpenEval highlights systematic genotyping across developmental stages documenting embryonic loss timing, while peer reviewers consistently acknowledge placental insufficiency leading to IUGR and accept fetal/placental weight data.

Both support the placental insufficiency mechanism (C11, C138-C139). OpenEval views the timing correlation with placental nutrition switch as observational but compelling, while peer reviewers accept aberrant junctional zone development as the likely cause of placental insufficiency.

Both support fetal loss and reduced birth weight (C13-C14). OpenEval emphasizes statistical analysis with appropriate tests, while peer reviewers acknowledge comprehensive evaluation of fetal loss across pregnancy stages and genotyping data showing sub-Mendelian ratios.

Both support the developmental timing analysis (C121-C125). OpenEval emphasizes systematic genotyping at multiple stages clearly documenting timing of embryonic loss, while peer reviewers view comprehensive evaluation across pregnancy stages as valuable and accept the data supporting placental insufficiency.

Both support fetal characterization findings (C129-C137). OpenEval notes fetal measurements, metabolic parameters, and IGF signaling are consistent with IUGR, while peer reviewers accept these as supporting the IUGR phenotype as part of comprehensive analysis.

Both support the junctional zone defects (C12, C147-C150). OpenEval emphasizes quantitative morphometry with strong statistical evidence (p<0.0001), while peer reviewers explicitly accept aberrant junctional zone development and view discovery of SPAG7's role in placental establishment as a key achievement.

Both support placental characterization findings (C142-C146). OpenEval highlights CD34 staining and vascular gene expression ruling out vascular defects, with increased mtDNA interpreted as compensatory, while peer reviewers accept these as supporting placental insufficiency mechanism without specific discussion.

Both support SPAG7 expression pattern information (C140-C141). OpenEval views these as appropriately cited background providing context, while peer reviewers accept this as contextual information supporting placental and developmental phenotypes.

Both support organ and body composition findings (C45, C47-C49, C55-C58). OpenEval includes these as part of multiple converging measurements with DEXA and tissue weights, while peer reviewers acknowledge decreased organ sizes and lean body mass as part of comprehensive phenotyping.

Both support adipose tissue characterization (C50-C53). OpenEval emphasizes tissue weights and histology as part of robust phenotype characterization, while peer reviewers accept increased fat mass and adipose depot sizes with histological findings as supporting the obesity phenotype.

Both support liver findings (C59-C61). OpenEval clearly shows lipid accumulation without significant liver damage (n=4), while peer reviewers accept liver findings as part of metabolic characterization supporting the obesity phenotype.

Both support the hepatic steatosis observation (C61). OpenEval emphasizes this is clearly shown with appropriate sample size and notes lipid accumulation occurs without significant liver damage, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the metabolic phenotype.

Both support plasma lipid measurements (C63-C65). OpenEval includes these as part of converging measurements for metabolic dysfunction, while peer reviewers accept these as part of extensive physiological parameters measured, viewing them as supporting data.

Both support metabolic interpretations (C69). OpenEval views these as reasonable interpretations consistent with measured data and standard metabolic disease pathophysiology, while peer reviewers accept the metabolic dysfunction findings without challenging the interpretations.

Both support organ weight interpretations (C49). OpenEval views these as reasonable interpretations appropriately cautious in language, while peer reviewers accept organ size findings as part of comprehensive phenotyping.

Both support adipose tissue interpretations (C54). OpenEval views these as consistent with established knowledge and measured data, while peer reviewers accept adipose characterization as supporting the obesity phenotype.

Both support liver pathology interpretations (C62). OpenEval views these as reasonable interpretations aligning with standard understanding, while peer reviewers accept liver findings without challenging the interpretation about damage severity.

Both support plasma lipid interpretations (C66). OpenEval views these as appropriately cautious interpretations consistent with metabolic disease pathophysiology, while peer reviewers accept plasma lipid measurements as part of metabolic characterization.

Both support the lack of hyperphagia observation (C182-C183). OpenEval views this as an important distinction and reasonable speculation about counter-regulation, while peer reviewers accept this as distinguishing the model and supporting that energy expenditure drives obesity.

Both support the therapeutic implications (C185-C186). OpenEval views the therapeutic speculation as appropriately cautious ('may provide'), while peer reviewers implicitly support this by emphasizing conceptual and practical implications, though specific therapeutic speculation is not directly addressed.

Both support broader implications for developmental programming (C200). OpenEval views therapeutic speculation as appropriately cautious, while peer reviewers support broader implications for understanding pregnancy disruptions' enduring impact on metabolic well-being of subsequent generations.

Both support the significance for understanding fetal-adult connections (C198-C199). OpenEval views the connection as demonstrated though precise molecular mechanisms remain to be elucidated, while peer reviewers emphasize significance from maternal-fetal medicine perspective and view as reasonable future direction.

Both support the forward genetic screen approach (C25). OpenEval views background claims as well-established and appropriately cited, while peer reviewers unanimously view the unbiased forward genetic screen as a major strength of the study.

Both support the background context about SPAG7 (C25). OpenEval emphasizes these are appropriately cited published literature providing necessary background, while peer reviewers acknowledge the forward genetic screen that identified SPAG7 as a strength.

OpenEval supports background claims about obesity epidemiology and therapy limitations (C18-C24) as well-established facts providing study rationale. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses these background claims.

OpenEval supports background literature about SPAG7's associations with various diseases (C26-C40) as appropriately cited, noting the knowledge gap this study addresses. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically discusses this background literature.

OpenEval supports background claims about IUGR, placental development, and developmental programming (C132, C153-C177) as appropriately cited and well-grounded in literature. No corresponding peer review evaluation specifically addresses this background discussion.
